paragraphs: An autoencoder turns an image into a compact latent vector and reconstructs an image from that vector. This makes interpolation seem straightforward: combine two images’ vectors and decode the result. Yet intermediate vectors can produce distorted or implausible images. The paper attributes this problem to the geometry of the learned latent space.

The proposed method adds a regularization term that shapes this space around the training images. It encourages the underlying manifold—the set of latent representations consistent with the images—to be smooth and locally convex. The aim is to make nearby combinations of representations remain compatible with the structure of the data.

The authors demonstrate faithful image interpolation using this regularization. Their contribution connects reconstruction quality between examples to how the representation is organized, rather than treating interpolation as an operation applied after training. They also identify broader uses for the same technique: reducing overfitting and generating additional examples for data augmentation. These are presented as possible applications of the regularizer.
icml-2021-autoencoder-image-interpolatio.tldr: Shaping an autoencoder’s latent space to be smooth and locally convex supports more faithful interpolation between images.

paragraphs: Many difficult combinatorial tasks can be written as integer programs. Their cost terms specify which solutions are preferred, while their constraints specify which solutions are allowed. The paper explores how a neural network can learn both parts, bringing structured algorithmic reasoning into a system that also learns representations from raw inputs.

CombOptNet incorporates integer programming solvers as layers in a neural architecture. The overall system is trainable from end to end: feature extraction and the formulation of the combinatorial problem are learned together. A state-of-the-art solver then solves the learned problem. Learning constraints is central because those constraints express the problem’s combinatorial structure, rather than merely assigning scores to a fixed set of possibilities.

The authors investigate these layers through an extensive analysis on synthetic data and a demonstration on a competitive computer vision keypoint matching benchmark. These evaluations support the potential of jointly learning a representation and the optimization problem it feeds. The contribution is an integration of learning and solving; the abstract does not claim that learning removes the underlying computational difficulty of integer programming.
icml-2021-comboptnet-fit-the-right-np-ha.tldr: CombOptNet makes integer programming layers learn both costs and constraints alongside neural features.

paragraphs: A treatment’s average effect does not describe every way it can change outcomes. This paper studies conditional distributional treatment effects, which capture differences beyond the mean while accounting for conditioning information. Its starting point is a formal definition based on a distance between probability distributions, giving the broader question a mathematical target.

The authors then develop an instance based on maximum mean discrepancy, using kernel conditional mean embeddings to represent conditional distributions. Combined with a hypothesis test, this construction addresses whether there is evidence of a conditional distributional treatment effect. It separates detecting a difference from describing the particular form that difference takes.

To investigate that form, the paper offers two complementary tools. A conditional witness function supports exploratory analysis of distributional differences, while U-statistic regression quantifies effects involving higher-order moments, extending the familiar focus on conditional averages. Experiments with synthetic, semi-synthetic, and real datasets demonstrate the approach’s merits. Together, the components provide a framework for asking whether treatment changes an outcome distribution and then examining how it changes.
icml-2021-conditional-distributional-tre.tldr: The paper develops tools to detect and characterize conditional treatment effects beyond changes in average outcomes.

paragraphs: Q-learning estimates the value of actions using updates that include a maximum over estimated values. That maximization can create overestimation and lead to poor decisions. Double-Q-learning uses two estimators to address this problem, but it can instead underestimate values. The paper emphasizes that either direction of error can harm behavior in certain settings.

Ensemble Bootstrapped Q-Learning extends the two-estimator idea to an ensemble, with the goal of reducing estimation bias. The theoretical analysis studies a related statistical problem: estimating the largest mean among independent random variables. For that setting, the authors prove that updates of the proposed type yield lower mean squared error.

The empirical analysis demonstrates domains in which both overestimation and underestimation produce suboptimal performance. A deep reinforcement learning version of the method also outperforms other deep Q-learning algorithms on a suite of Atari games. These findings support using ensembles to improve value estimation, while keeping the theoretical claim tied to its stated statistical setting and the performance claim tied to the evaluated games.
icml-2021-ensemble-bootstrapping-for-q-l.tldr: Ensemble Bootstrapped Q-Learning extends Double-Q-learning to reduce estimation bias and improves performance on evaluated Atari games.

paragraphs: Learning in a sequential game does not automatically make strategies settle at an equilibrium. This paper studies Follow the Regularized Leader dynamics in games where players have imperfect information. Its starting concern is recurrence: learning trajectories can return near earlier states, so continued updating need not produce convergence to a single solution.

The authors extend existing recurrence results from normal-form games to two-player zero-sum games with imperfect information and other sequential settings. They then examine a way to change this behavior by adding a regularization term to the game’s rewards. For monotone games, this reward adaptation provides strong convergence guarantees.

The paper further shows how the reward adaptation can be used to construct algorithms that converge exactly to a Nash equilibrium. This connects an analysis of why learning can keep revisiting earlier behavior with a method for obtaining convergence. The authors also use the insights to build model-free algorithms described as state of the art for two-player zero-sum imperfect-information games. The convergence claims retain their stated game-class qualifications.
icml-2021-from-poincare-recurrence-to-co.tldr: Regularizing game rewards turns insights about recurring learning dynamics into equilibrium-convergent algorithms for specified game classes.

paragraphs: Neural architecture search commonly separates two decisions: fitting network weights on training data and selecting architecture-related hyperparameters on validation data. When many candidate networks can fit the training data perfectly, training loss offers little help in choosing among them. This paper investigates why validation-based selection can still support good performance on unseen data.

The analysis shows that properties of validation loss, including risk and hyper-gradients, can indicate corresponding properties of true test loss. Hyper-gradients describe how the validation objective changes with hyperparameters. The guarantees apply to continuous search spaces, which matter for differentiable architecture search, and establish protection against overfitting with a near-minimal validation sample size.

The authors also derive generalization bounds with particular attention to searching over activation choices and using gradient-based methods. They connect architecture search to low-rank matrix learning, obtaining algorithmic insights from that relationship. In the analyzed setting, spectral methods can accurately learn the upper-level solution and achieve near-minimal risk. The contribution therefore addresses both the statistical role of validation data and methods for carrying out the search.
icml-2021-generalization-guarantees-for-.tldr: The paper gives generalization guarantees for validation-based architecture search and connects its optimization to low-rank matrix learning.

paragraphs: This paper develops a generative adversarial network for stochastic sequences governed by Markovian temporal dynamics. The modeling goal concerns how data evolve over time, including randomness in that evolution. Capturing these dynamics requires a generator that represents temporal transitions and a discriminator that evaluates structure across both space and time.

The proposed conditional generator is based on a stochastic differential equation. It is paired with discriminator networks subject to spatial and temporal constraints. Because the generator and discriminator learn through a competing min-max objective, the authors also introduce well-posed constraint terms for both networks to stabilize their learning dynamics. These components address sequence generation and training stability together.

The paper additionally introduces a conditional Markov Wasserstein distance that induces a pathwise Wasserstein distance, connecting comparisons of conditional dynamics with comparisons of whole trajectories. Experiments across several data types show the method outperforming state-of-the-art methods in those evaluations. The stated contribution combines a stochastic model of temporal evolution, constraints for adversarial learning, and a distributional distance suited to the sequential setting.
icml-2021-generative-adversarial-network.tldr: A GAN combines stochastic differential equation generation, constrained discrimination, and a Markov Wasserstein distance to model random temporal dynamics.

paragraphs: In unlabeled sensing, linear measurements are available but their ordering has been changed by an unknown permutation. Homomorphic sensing generalizes this situation: the measurements undergo an unknown linear transformation selected from a known finite set. The central question is when the original signal remains uniquely recoverable despite uncertainty about that transformation.

The paper gives simpler and tighter conditions for a unique solution and shows that the solution is locally stable under noise. It also establishes that sparsity allows uniqueness under less demanding conditions. Here sparsity means that the signal has only a limited number of nonzero components, providing additional structure for resolving the measurement ambiguity.

Applying this theory to unlabeled compressed sensing yields, under mild conditions, the existence of a unique sparsest solution. The authors also present an iterative algorithm for that problem and validate it with synthetic experiments. Finally, they use the general framework to connect unlabeled sensing with other practical problems. The results distinguish theoretical recoverability and local noise stability from the separate empirical validation of an algorithm.
icml-2021-homomorphic-sensing-sparsity-a.tldr: The paper strengthens uniqueness and local noise-stability results for sensing with unknown transformations, including improved conditions for sparse signals.

paragraphs: The paper argues that learning program meaning requires attention to how programs operate, beyond treating source code as language-like text. Programming-language theory provides an explicit account through operational semantics: a program changes an environment, such as memory contents, through operations including reads, writes, and conditional branches.

This motivates a learning paradigm with two sources of information. One represents fundamental operations in a form aligned with operational semantics. The other describes how the environment changes, which the authors regard as essential to understanding programs. Their model, OSCAR, implements this idea with hierarchical Transformer pretraining using intermediate representations and an encoding derived from static analysis.

The intermediate representation supplies the operational view, while static analysis approximates environment transitions. That approximation is part of the proposed approach, rather than a claim that all runtime behavior is directly observed. Across practical software engineering tasks, OSCAR empirically demonstrates strong program-semantics understanding. The contribution links the choice of pretraining information to a formal account of program meaning and supports that design through downstream task performance.
icml-2021-how-could-neural-networks-unde.tldr: OSCAR learns program representations from fundamental operations and approximated environment transitions inspired by operational semantics.

paragraphs: Network regression explains the values of relationships using information about individual actors or pairs of actors. Such models appear in social and biological research. For their conclusions to be reliable, they must account for dependencies among the unexplained parts of those relationships, because the edges of a network need not provide independent information.

The paper focuses on a weakness of common error models: they assume a degree of homogeneity that can overlook natural communities among actors. The proposed framework instead models residual dependence through community structure. This makes the organization of the network part of the statistical description of what remains unexplained by the predictors.

The authors use exchangeability properties arising from that community-based error distribution to obtain parsimonious standard errors for regression coefficients. These properties allow relevant relations to share statistical structure, avoiding an unrestricted description of every dependence. The contribution concerns inference: assessing uncertainty about regression parameters in a way that acknowledges clustering among actors. Its central message is that community structure matters not only for describing a network, but also for quantifying uncertainty in explanations of its edges.
icml-2021-inference-for-network-regressi.tldr: A network regression framework uses community-based residual dependence to construct parsimonious standard errors for model coefficients.

paragraphs: This paper combines text generation and classification through a shared latent representation. A generator produces a text sequence from a continuous vector. An energy-based prior links that vector to a discrete category represented by a one-hot symbol, allowing category information to be inferred from an observed example through its continuous representation.

The link also supports information bottleneck regularization. This encourages the continuous vector to retain information about the example that is useful for identifying its underlying category. The category-vector relationship, generator, and inference network are learned jointly, so the representation’s organization develops alongside the mechanisms that interpret and generate text.

Training can proceed without category labels or in a semi-supervised setting where only some examples have labels. Experiments show a meaningful, well-structured latent space that supports both effective classification and generation with high quality, diversity, and interpretability. The stated findings suggest that coupling symbolic categories with continuous representations can serve both tasks within one learned model, including settings with limited or absent category supervision.
icml-2021-latent-space-energy-based-mode.tldr: An energy-based prior couples continuous text representations with discrete categories to support generation and classification with limited or no labels.

paragraphs: A linear contextual bandit chooses actions using a representation of the available context. The same problem can have several valid linear representations, and that choice can strongly affect regret—the cumulative cost of decisions relative to the benchmark. This paper studies how a learner can benefit from favorable representations without being given the best one in advance.

The authors first organize and analyze existing definitions of a good representation. They then propose an algorithm that selects among M candidates. Its regret is no worse than running LinUCB with the best candidate, up to a logarithmic factor in M. Consequently, when the candidate set contains a good representation, the algorithm achieves constant problem-dependent regret.

A further result shows that constant regret may still be possible when no initial candidate is individually good: the algorithm can implicitly construct a good representation. This is a possibility established by the analysis, not a claim for every candidate set. Experiments on standard contextual bandit problems validate the theoretical findings and highlight representation selection as part of the learning problem.
icml-2021-leveraging-good-representation.tldr: A representation-selection algorithm approaches the best candidate’s regret and achieves constant regret when suitable representation structure is available.

paragraphs: In games with strategic cycles, one strategy can defeat another while losing to a third, so there may be no consistent winner. Maintaining varied behaviors is therefore important. This paper develops a geometric account of behavioral diversity and a metric based on determinantal point processes, making diversity an explicit part of the learning objective.

The authors incorporate the metric into best-response dynamics to produce diverse fictitious play and a diverse policy-space response oracle. They prove uniqueness of the diverse best response and convergence of their algorithms on two-player games. They also show that maximizing the diversity metric guarantees expansion of the gamescape, the convex region spanned by agents’ mixtures of strategies.

The methods are evaluated on tens of games with strong non-transitivity. Results suggest exploitability is at least as good as that of PSRO solvers, and lower in most tested games, through discovery of effective and varied strategies. The contribution connects a formal diversity measure, a geometric guarantee, and empirical resistance to exploitation, rather than relying solely on an informal preference for varied behavior.
icml-2021-modelling-behavioural-diversit.tldr: A geometric diversity metric guides game-learning algorithms toward broader strategy sets and lower exploitability in most evaluated games.

paragraphs: Neural differential equations let an adaptive numerical solver determine how many computation steps are needed. This flexibility can make prediction expensive when the learned dynamics require many network evaluations. Existing approaches to accelerating prediction can themselves impose substantial training costs through high-order automatic differentiation.

The paper proposes using information already produced inside adaptive solvers to guide training toward dynamics that are easier to solve. Its regularizer draws on local error estimates and stiffness heuristics as inexpensive estimates of computational difficulty. Combined with discrete adjoint sensitivities, these signals make the solver’s internal numerical knowledge part of the learning process.

The method fits into the underlying neural differential equation framework without changing it and extends from ordinary to stochastic differential equations. The authors demonstrate that it can halve prediction time while producing a similar reduction in training time. Those are demonstrated gains, rather than guaranteed speedups for every model. The broader contribution is to connect what the numerical solver finds difficult with what the neural model is encouraged to learn.
icml-2021-opening-the-blackbox-accelerat.tldr: Regularizing neural differential equations with solver-internal cost estimates can reduce both prediction and training time.

paragraphs: Counterfactual explanations identify changes to an input that would produce a different model outcome. Heuristic searches can depend on where they start and lack guarantees about solution quality. This paper formulates explanation search for tree ensembles as a mathematical optimization problem with explicit objectives and constraints.

The authors develop efficient mixed-integer programming approaches and incorporate isolation forests to favor plausible explanations with low outlier scores. Their framework also supports different data types, structural restrictions on the feature space, resource limits, and actionability requirements. These constraints let the optimization reflect which proposed changes are permitted or practical within the chosen model.

In experiments, the approach requires orders of magnitude less computational effort than previous mathematical programming methods. It scales to large datasets and tree ensembles, producing explanations within seconds and solving the specified models to optimality. Here optimality is grounded in the defined objective and constraints. The contribution is a systematic, configurable search procedure whose explanations can be assessed against an explicit model of what makes a counterfactual desirable.
icml-2021-optimal-counterfactual-explana.tldr: Efficient mixed-integer optimization produces optimal tree-ensemble counterfactuals under explicit plausibility, structural, and actionability constraints.

paragraphs: Choosing a sparse network before training can improve the efficiency of learning and inference. This paper builds on a decomposition of the Neural Tangent Kernel that separates a data-dependent component from an architecture-dependent Path Kernel. That framework had motivated Synflow-L2, a method for constructing networks with favorable convergence properties without training data.

The authors identify a tradeoff: although Synflow-L2 is optimal in terms of convergence at a given density, it creates narrow bottleneck layers. These subnetworks perform poorly compared with other data-independent methods using the same number of parameters. Favorable convergence properties alone therefore do not settle how a sparse network should distribute its connections.

PHEW constructs sparse networks through biased random walks based only on their initial weights. It retains similar Path Kernel properties while producing wider layers, resulting in better generalization and performance. The reported evaluations show significant gains over SynFlow and SynFlow-L2 across a wide range of network densities. The contribution combines a data-free construction procedure with attention to layer width as well as convergence.
icml-2021-phew-constructing-sparse-netwo.tldr: PHEW uses initial-weight-based random walks to construct sparse networks with wider layers and improved generalization without training data.

paragraphs: Video classification can require sharing sensitive personal footage, while a classifier’s owner may also want to keep model parameters private. This paper develops a pipeline that lets a party infer a video label without requiring the video or model parameters to be disclosed to other entities in plaintext.

The approach builds on secure multi-party computation protocols for private image classification. The authors add protocols for oblivious single-frame selection and secure aggregation of labels across frames. Together, these components support the full video classification process using a method that classifies individual frames, extending protection beyond the image classifier to frame selection and combination of results.

The system is evaluated for private human emotion recognition across several security settings. These include honest- and dishonest-majority configurations among the computing parties, as well as passive and active adversaries. The reported results achieve state-of-the-art classification accuracy without leaking sensitive user information in those settings. The contribution is an end-to-end secure implementation that protects both the video owner’s input and the classifier owner’s parameters under the considered configurations.
icml-2021-privacy-preserving-video-class.tldr: Secure multi-party computation enables video classification while protecting both footage and model parameters in the evaluated security settings.

paragraphs: A predictor can perform well on familiar data yet respond poorly when hidden causes change. This paper studies linear prediction when those causes cannot be observed directly but noisy proxy measurements are available. It introduces regularization that trades some in-distribution predictive performance for robustness to causal interventions on the unobserved variables.

Under a linear structural causal model, the authors show that one proxy is enough to construct estimators that are prediction optimal for interventions of bounded strength. The scope of that protection depends on the proxy’s measurement noise. Because this noise magnitude is generally not identifiable, the corresponding intervention strength need not be known.

With two proxies, a modified estimator achieves prediction optimality for interventions up to a known strength. The authors also extend the estimators to use information available during training about the intervention expected at test time. Synthetic experiments and hourly pollution data from several Chinese cities evaluate the theoretical findings. The distinction between one and two proxies matters because it changes whether the robustness range can be specified.
icml-2021-regularizing-towards-causal-in.tldr: Proxy-based regularization gives linear predictors intervention-robustness guarantees whose identifiable range improves when two proxies are available.

paragraphs: Rissanen Data Analysis asks whether a particular capability helps explain a dataset’s labels from its inputs. The paper imagines a labeling program built from subroutines with different capabilities. It posits that a capability is useful exactly when the shortest program that uses it is shorter than the shortest program that does not.

The length of a truly minimal program cannot be computed, so the method estimates the labels’ minimum description length as a proxy. This converts an abstract question about useful computational capabilities into a practical dataset-analysis approach. The comparison is framed around how compactly the labels can be described when a capability is available versus when it is absent.

The authors demonstrate applications across natural-language processing. These include assessing whether generating subquestions helps answer a question, evaluating rationales and explanations, examining the contribution of different parts of speech, and uncovering gender bias in datasets. The contribution is a common analytical framework for these questions, grounded in description length while explicitly relying on an estimate of an uncomputable ideal.
icml-2021-rissanen-data-analysis-examini.tldr: Rissanen Data Analysis estimates description length to assess which capabilities help explain a dataset’s labels.

paragraphs: Spatio-temporal forecasting involves data whose behavior depends on both time and relationships across locations or entities. Deep models can capture these dependencies, but accurate point predictions do not describe uncertainty. This paper develops a probabilistic forecasting approach that treats the observed time series as a random realization of a nonlinear state-space model.

The method targets Bayesian inference over hidden states: it seeks a distribution of plausible underlying states rather than a single estimate. Particle flow approximates the posterior distribution of those states. The authors use it because of its effectiveness in complex, high-dimensional settings, making uncertainty about hidden dynamics a central part of the forecasting process.

Experiments on several real-world time-series datasets show better characterization of uncertainty while maintaining accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art point forecasting methods. This pairing matters because a richer account of predictive uncertainty is useful alongside a competitive central forecast. The reported finding is that the approach supplies that additional probabilistic information without sacrificing comparable point-prediction accuracy in the evaluated settings.
icml-2021-rnn-with-particle-flow-for-pro.tldr: Particle-flow inference over nonlinear hidden states improves forecast uncertainty characterization while retaining competitive point-prediction accuracy.

paragraphs: This paper considers contextual bandits with many available features but only a small subset that affects rewards. A learner must make decisions while discovering which information is useful. Existing sparse-bandit methods commonly require the number of relevant features in advance, even though that quantity is rarely known in practice.

The proposed algorithm removes the need to supply this sparsity index. That matters because specifying the wrong number can severely degrade existing methods’ performance. Under conditions described as mild, the authors establish tight regret bounds, giving theoretical control over the accumulated cost of the algorithm’s decisions without assuming prior knowledge of the relevant feature count.

A comprehensive numerical evaluation reports that the method consistently outperforms existing approaches. The comparison even gives those approaches the correct sparsity index while withholding it from the proposed algorithm. These results support the practical value of adapting without that input, alongside the conditional theoretical guarantees. The contribution is specifically about learning in sparse high-dimensional bandits without requiring the sparsity level to be known beforehand.
icml-2021-sparsity-agnostic-lasso-bandit.tldr: A sparse contextual-bandit algorithm achieves tight regret bounds without knowing how many features affect rewards.

paragraphs: Compressing a neural network can make adversarial robustness harder to maintain. This paper addresses training networks with few connections while explicitly optimizing robustness. Its approach keeps the network sparse throughout training, avoiding the need to first train a dense network and then prune connections to reach the desired connectivity budget.

The method uses a rewiring process motivated by Bayesian posterior sampling. It jointly learns which connections to retain and the tradeoff between accuracy and robustness under an adversarial learning objective. Global connectivity constraints remain satisfied throughout optimization, so sparsity governs the training process itself rather than appearing only in the final model.

Benchmark experiments show performance superior to recently proposed robustness-aware pruning methods that begin with dense networks. The result is especially relevant to the paper’s focus on high sparsity: it demonstrates that the evaluated robust-learning objectives can work with dynamically changing sparse connectivity. The contribution combines a constrained network structure with learned rewiring, supporting adversarially robust training without dense pretraining in the reported comparisons.
icml-2021-training-adversarially-robust-.tldr: Bayesian connectivity sampling trains adversarially robust networks while keeping them sparse throughout optimization.

paragraphs: Neural activation coding learns representations from unlabeled data by focusing on the patterns of activity inside an encoder. The authors argue that downstream predictors benefit when an encoder makes full use of its nonlinear expressive capacity. Their objective maximizes mutual information between the data and activation patterns transmitted through a noisy communication channel.

The analysis shows that learning activation codes robust to this noise increases the number of distinct linear regions in a ReLU encoder, and therefore its maximum nonlinear expressivity. The method learns both continuous and discrete representations. This provides two ways to use the learned information, which the paper evaluates through different downstream tasks.

Continuous representations are tested through linear classification on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-1K, while discrete representations are tested through nearest-neighbor retrieval on CIFAR-10 and FLICKR-25K. Results are better than or comparable to recent baselines, including SimCLR and DistillHash. The authors also report significant benefits from NAC pretraining for deep generative models. These findings connect an activation-based training objective with usefulness across several evaluated applications.
icml-2021-unsupervised-representation-le.tldr: Neural activation coding learns noise-robust activation patterns that support useful continuous and discrete representations without labels.

paragraphs: Planning becomes more difficult when an action has several possible consequences or the agent cannot observe the full environment. This paper extends model-based reinforcement learning to these stochastic and partially observable settings. Its central idea is to represent the different possible effects of an action using discrete latent variables learned by an autoencoder.

A stochastic variant of Monte Carlo tree search then plans over both the agent’s choices and the latent variables describing the environment’s response. This gives the planning procedure an explicit representation of alternative outcomes. The learned discrete representation connects the model of environmental uncertainty to the branches considered during search.

The method significantly outperforms an offline version of MuZero on a stochastic interpretation of chess in which the opponent is treated as part of the environment. It also scales to DeepMind Lab, a first-person three-dimensional environment with large visual observations and partial observability. Together, these demonstrations support the approach in settings involving uncertain responses and incomplete observations, with the comparison to MuZero specifically tied to the evaluated chess setup.
icml-2021-vector-quantized-models-for-pl.tldr: Discrete autoencoders represent uncertain action outcomes so tree search can plan in stochastic and partially observable environments.

paragraphs: Learning with noisy labels often uses small training loss to identify examples considered more reliable. This paper examines that practice through distributionally robust optimization. It studies the distributional relationship between samples treated as certain and uncertain under small-loss criteria, seeking a theoretical basis for extracting useful information from the uncertain group.

The proposed Wasserstein distributional normalization moves uncertain samples into a robustly certified region. It uses nonparametric Wasserstein gradient flows of the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck type, described as inexpensive and fast to implement. The purpose is to use the relationship between the two sample groups to make uncertain examples useful for classification.

The authors establish a fundamental correlation between network confidence and distributional certification and provide a concentration inequality when the network escapes overparameterization. Experiments on Clothing1M and CIFAR-10/100 with diverse noisy labels show the nonparametric classification method outperforming the compared parametric baselines. The contribution combines a theoretical interpretation of small-loss selection with a distributional transformation designed to recover value from uncertain training examples.
icml-2021-wasserstein-distributional-nor.tldr: Wasserstein distributional normalization uses robust optimization to turn uncertain noisy-label samples into useful classification information.
